newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Forex loss may cut Senchem yr shr by 30 pct.
newsitem.headline: Forex loss may cut Senchem yr shr by 30 pct.

text.p: South African chemical firm Sentrachem Ltd's earnings could sink by 30 percent next year, reeling from the twin blows of a subsidiary's heavy forward exchange loss and an expected lame performance.

Analysts said on Thursday they had downgraded their forecasts for the 1996/97 year after a shock announcement by Sentrachem that a poor forward cover decision by its Sanachem operation would strip 60 cents off group earnings per share in the year to August 1997.
In the year to August 31 1996, the group posted pre-exceptional earnings of 131.2 cents per share.
But the damage to group profits could be even greater as Sanachem, a manufacturer and exporter of pesticides, battled with operational problems.
"The foreign exchange issue is limited to 60 cents a share...(but) for operational reasons there could be a further way to go," John Job, managing director of Sentrachem, told Reuters on Thursday.

As the profit warning rippled through the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, shares lost over a third of their value, plunging to a weakest level of 800 cents. They had since recovered slightly to trade at 940 cents.

Themi Themistocleous, an analyst at SBC Warburg, said currency losses arose from a decision to buy back forward cover, representing 18 months' export trade, which had been taken out at a rate much lower than the current spot rate.
This had cost Sanachem some 185 million rand, he said.

"Instead of selling (their products) at a lower rate until the cover runs out, they decided to unwind the cover...Their earnings will be sharply down next year, it might be by 30 percent," Themistocleous said.
Another analyst who asked not to be identified said earnings could sink to around 96 cents a share.
Analysts said currency losses may not have been taken on the chin had Sanachem looked set to post robust profits. These could have been use to cushion the forex losses, they said.
Themistocleous said problems at Sanachem included high levels of working capital and chasing turnover at the expense of margins.
Other analysts said Sanachem may recently have run up against stiff market competition.
"Sanachem used to operate in a market with few competitors. There may be more piling in on this nice margin area and extra capacity coming on," one said.
Another analyst said environmental concerns around Sanachem's operation may again have flared up. "It is possible losses could be incurred from capital expenditure to clean that up," he said.
